subject: clocked request/acknowledge handshake

source.standard: four-phase (return-to-zero) request/acknowledge handshake convention; digital timing-diagram reading conventions
source.locator: four-phase / return-to-zero handshake protocol: phase 1 request asserts, phase 2 acknowledge asserts in response, phase 3 request de-asserts in response to acknowledge, phase 4 acknowledge de-asserts in response to request's de-assertion

authored.protocol: source-first: the author agent worked only from the handshake convention and never saw the .fd file

questions.ask: Of the four lanes in this diagram, one signal toggles at a constant, regular rate for the entire duration, independent of whatever the request/acknowledge/completion signals are doing. Which signal is that?
questions.tests: identifies the clock lane as the one periodic, free-running signal versus the event-driven req/ack/done signals
questions.source_locator: digital timing-diagram convention: a clock lane is periodic and independent of handshake state
questions.answer: The clock (clk) — it toggles at a fixed, regular rate throughout the whole diagram, while req, ack, and done only change in response to handshake events.

questions.ask: At the very start of the diagram, before any handshake has begun, what level (high or low) are the request, acknowledge, and completion signals resting at?
questions.tests: idle/reset level of the non-clock lanes at the start of a return-to-zero handshake
questions.source_locator: four-phase handshake convention: all handshake lines idle low before phase 1 begins
questions.answer: All three (req, ack, done) are low / de-asserted at the start; only the clock lane is active, toggling.

questions.ask: In one full handshake cycle, which signal transitions (asserts) first: the request or the acknowledge?
questions.tests: identifies request as the initiating signal of the four-phase handshake, not acknowledge
questions.source_locator: four-phase handshake convention, phase 1: requester asserts request first
questions.answer: The request (req) asserts first; the acknowledge (ack) only asserts afterward, in response.

questions.ask: Can the acknowledge signal assert (go high) before the request signal has asserted? Explain why or why not.
questions.tests: causal dependence: ack's rise is a response to req's rise, so ack cannot precede req
questions.source_locator: four-phase handshake convention, phase 2: acknowledge is a response to a request that has already asserted
questions.answer: No. Ack's rising transition is caused by / responds to req's rising transition, so ack cannot go high until after req has already gone high; ack depends on req, not the other way around.

questions.ask: What causes the request signal to return to its low (idle) level after the handshake has begun?
questions.tests: req's fall is a response to ack's rise (phase 3 of the four-phase handshake), not a free-running or self-timed event
questions.source_locator: four-phase handshake convention, phase 3: requester withdraws request upon seeing acknowledge
questions.answer: The request returns low in response to the acknowledge going high — req de-asserts because it has seen ack asserted, not on its own.

questions.ask: What causes the acknowledge signal to return to its low (idle) level?
questions.tests: ack's fall is a response to req's fall (phase 4 of the four-phase handshake), completing the return-to-zero cycle
questions.source_locator: four-phase handshake convention, phase 4: responder withdraws acknowledge upon seeing request withdrawn
questions.answer: Ack returns low in response to req having already returned low — the acknowledge de-asserts because it sees the request was withdrawn, completing the four-phase return-to-zero cycle.

questions.ask: What does the completion signal indicate, and when does it occur relative to the request/acknowledge exchange?
questions.tests: completion/done asserts after the req/ack handshake cycle has finished, not partway through it
questions.source_locator: handshake convention: a completion/done indicator marks the end of the req/ack exchange
questions.answer: The completion (done) signal asserts after the request/acknowledge handshake cycle has finished — once req and ack have both returned to idle — signaling that the transaction is complete.

questions.ask: List, in order, the four transitions that make up one complete four-phase handshake cycle: which signal moves, and in which direction, at each step?
questions.tests: the full ordered sequence of the four-phase handshake: req rises, ack rises, req falls, ack falls
questions.source_locator: four-phase (return-to-zero) handshake convention, all four phases
questions.answer: 1) req goes high (asserts); 2) ack goes high (asserts) in response; 3) req goes low (de-asserts) in response to ack; 4) ack goes low (de-asserts) in response to req's fall, returning both signals to idle.
